extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, research mathematicians, and undergraduate/graduate students learning to read and write mathematical proofs (especially for publication)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the conventional genre features for writing mathematical proofs (as used by research mathematicians and for publication), describing expectations about structure, notation, verbosity, and rhetorical devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs are not reports of the proving process
rubrics_metrics.description: Final written proofs do not record the process of discovery (no false starts, failed attempts, or step-by-step diary of what the author tried); one generally does not write things like 'I tried this and it did not work' or (usually) 'I want to show...' except possibly in very long, complicated proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors present the polished product: the correct statement with a clean proof. Historical development, false starts, mistakes, or the creative process are typically omitted. Example anti-patterns: including 'I tried this' comments or narrating failed approaches. Citations: Csiszar (2003) and Ewing (1984) quoted on expecting a polished product rather than a record of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs contain little redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical proofs prize brevity, conciseness, and precision of meaning and avoid redundant restatements or arguing the same point from multiple viewpoints within the same proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repeating the argument from another point of view in the same proof. Remove irrelevancies and trivia; be concise. Halmos' advice: 'Down with the Irrelevant and Trivia'—do not include chit-chat or irrelevant phrases. Anti-patterns: philosophical-style repetition or restating the same argument in several ways inside one proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols are introduced one-to-one with mathematical objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols should generally correspond one-to-one with mathematical objects; the same symbol should not be used to represent different objects (except across independent subproofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reuse symbols for different numbers or objects in the same proof, as this causes confusion for validators. Example anti-pattern: unnecessary profusion of letters (introducing many new symbols without need) as seen in a student proof that used j,k,l unnecessarily for m,n,p.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs contain only minimal explanations of inferences (warrants often implicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine computations and obvious inferences may be omitted; warrants for simple steps are often left implicit because they are clear to the intended reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit routine computations that do not depend on unexpected tricks. Indicate starting point, describe the procedure, and state the outcome rather than detailing every elementary inference. Editors/authors note that sometimes leaving an obvious reason out is more effective. Example: a student omitted an obvious warrant between steps—this is acceptable when the step is routine; do not omit nontrivial warrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs contain only very short overviews or advance organizers
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs typically include only brief signposts (e.g., 'Suppose to the contrary that...') and not detailed advance outlines of the entire proof's organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generally provide a full road-map of the proof's internal case structure or a lengthy hierarchical overview in advance; brief indicators are acceptable. Contrast: Leron's proposal for hierarchical structuring in classroom presentations; in published proofs the norm is short organizers to preserve flow and conciseness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire definitions (available outside the proof) are not quoted in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not restate full standard definitions inside proofs; rather reference them succinctly (e.g., 'By definition of continuity, ...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid quoting textbook-length definitions inside proofs as this distracts readers and slows reading. Use concise references to definitions; only include a full definition if the proof genuinely depends on a nonstandard formulation. Anti-pattern: students writing out the full epsilon-delta definition inside a proof instead of writing 'by definition'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs are 'logically concrete'—avoid universal quantifiers where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetorically prefer selecting a fixed but arbitrary element (e.g., 'Let x be...') rather than writing universal quantifiers like 'for all x' repeatedly; this simplifies the logic and aids the validator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the device of fixing an arbitrary element to keep the argument concrete and clear. Students often overuse 'for all x' or 'for all ε' inside proofs; the conventional style is to choose an arbitrary representative and reason about it. This rhetorical choice reduces cognitive load and potential errors for readers and graders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs present a polished, monological text that minimizes distractions to aid validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical proofs are presented as monological, polished texts that emphasize the inevitability or natural unfolding of the argument and minimize distracting details so validators can more easily find errors and follow the path of the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a presentation that lets readers 'see the path—not examine it with a microscope.' The rhetoric of inevitability and minimized distractions can provide reader pleasure and make validation as easy and reliable as possible. This overarching aim explains many of the specific conventions above (brevity, minimal warrants, avoidance of process reporting, etc.).
